prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in moire flat-band systems

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a discovery in the sense I weigh most: a short, exactly stated piece of theory (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, which gives a flat band at a specific twist angle) was followed by an experiment that found what the theory made plausible (correlated insulators and superconductivity in 2018), and a whole tunable platform for strongly correlated electrons followed. It is simple to state, hard to dismiss, and has been reproduced by many groups. Five of seven ranking members place it in their top three or better, so the support is broad rather than a single champion's preference, which I treat as weak evidence of merit but as useful evidence that the case survives scrutiny from different subfields.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and credit. The experiments are only about eight years old, the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and the prize would have to rest on flat bands and correlated phases rather than on a mechanism. On attribution, three slots must be shared among four credited names, and whoever is left out (Bistritzer, the junior author of the decisive theory, or Andrei, who has the earlier STM and transport evidence of flat bands) has a real claim. Topological insulators (B028) have two decades of confirmation and are the safer choice on timing.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks topological insulators first and argues that theory, the HgTe experiment and the 3D ARPES work form a complete chain from idea to observation, with roughly two decades of stable confirmation.
responses.response: I accept the maturity argument and the chain from idea to observation, and I rank B028 as my fallback. My reservation is the allocation. Kane-Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan leave out Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Moore-Balents, who are not on the credited list, so the prize would be an incomplete picture of the field. In B046 the decisive theory-plus-experiment pair is much cleaner. I do not think Hasan's inclusion resolves the problem, since it adds the 3D branch while still omitting Zhang's proposal.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first: a clean two-person credit (Katori for the magic-wavelength idea, Ye for record accuracy), many independent laboratories at the 1e-18 level, and a natural successor to the 2005 prize.
responses.response: I agree that B034 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and I ranked it third for that reason. I disagree that this should decide the question. A clear credit list does not make a discovery more fundamental, and the clock is an instrument-defining advance whose largest consequence, redefining the second, has not yet happened. Ye's frequency-comb work also overlaps with the 2005 prize, as you noted yourself. I would back it as the strongest precision-measurement option if the committee prefers a mature and tidy case, and I note your possible connection to the Hall laboratory environment.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, noting a rare case where a continuum band-structure prediction preceded and guided a field-defining experiment, and leans toward MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero with the third slot between Andrei and Bistritzer unresolved.
responses.response: I agree with the main argument and with the two-name core. On the third slot I favour Andrei, because her STM and transport evidence of flat bands and van Hove singularities is independent and precedes the 2018 experiments, which makes it more than an echo of the theory. Bistritzer's contribution is the same continuum model as MacDonald's and is already represented by the theory credit. I recognise this is a judgement about how the Academy treats junior co-authors, and I would not fight hard if the committee preferred Bistritzer.

responses.point: Johansson ranks topological insulators first and twisted bilayer graphene second, calling the latter slightly early because the superconducting pairing remains debated, and proposes the Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero set.
responses.response: I share the concern about the pairing mechanism and it is the main reason B046 is not an obvious first choice. I think a citation worded around flat bands and correlated phases avoids resting the prize on the mechanism. I disagree about Bistritzer: the continuum model carries both names, but crediting Bistritzer over Andrei would leave out the experimental line that independently preceded the 2018 work.

uncertainties: Whether Andrei or Bistritzer should hold the third place; the credited-name list does not settle priority.
Whether eight years since the 2018 experiments is enough time, given the open question of the superconducting pairing mechanism.
Whether the committee should prefer the more mature topological-insulator case (B028) and accept the allocation problem it carries (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Moore-Balents are not credited).
I rely on memory of the literature and have not checked priority dates beyond the supplied entries.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred configuration. I have no documented connection to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Andrei, and my own field (statistical physics of complex systems) is distant from moire materials.
